Abstract Dysregulated innate immune responses contribute to multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), characterized by gastrointestinal, mucocutaneous, and/or cardiovascular injury occurring weeks after severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) exposure. To investigate innate immune functions, we stimulated ex vivo peripheral blood cells from MIS-C patients with agonists of Toll-like receptors (TLR), key innate immune response initiators. We found severely dampened cytokine responses and elevated gene expression of negative regulators of TLR signaling. Increased plasma levels of zonulin, a gut leakage marker, were also detected. These effects were also observed in fully convalescent children months after MIS-C recovery. When we investigated the genetic background of patients in relation to TLR responsiveness, we found that cells from MIS-C children carrying rare heterozygous variants of lysosomal trafficking regulator (LYST) were less refractory to TLR stimulation and exhibited lysosomal and mitochondrial abnormalities with altered energy metabolism. Moreover, these rare LYST variant heterozygous carriers tended to exhibit unfavorable clinical laboratory indicators of inflammation, including more profound lymphopenia. The results of our observational study have several implications. First, TLR hyporesponsiveness may be associated with hyperinflammation and/or excessive or prolonged stimulation with gut-originated TLR ligands. Second, TLR hyporesponsiveness during MIS-C may be protective, since LYST variant heterozygous carriers exhibited reduced TLR hyporesponsiveness and unfavorable clinical laboratory indicators of inflammation. Thus, links may exist between genetic background, ability to establish a refractory immune state, and MIS-C clinical spectrum. Third, the possibility exists that prolonged TLR hyporesponsiveness is one of the mechanisms driving long coronavirus disease (COVID), which highlights the need to monitor long-term consequences of MIS-C. The most dramatic one is a rare syndrome with multiorgan involvement that manifests several weeks after infection with SARS-CoV-2. This clinical entity, named multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), was first reported in the United Kingdom early in the pandemic 5 and subsequently defined by the US Center for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization. 6 , 7 Symptoms of MIS-C include fever, rash, gastrointestinal symptoms, coagulopathy, myocardial dysfunction, and/or shock. 4 , 8 Underlying the clinical symptoms of MIS-C are multilineage immune activation and tissue inflammation, including increased gastrointestinal permeability, elevated circulating markers of microangiopathy, and release of troponin and natriuretic peptides, indicative of cardiac inflammation. 4 , 8 Among the immunological abnormalities reported for MIS-C, lymphopenia is most characteristic, as it separates MIS-C from the phenotypically similar Kawasaki disease and correlates with the degree of MIS-C severity. 4 , 8 Still, the mechanisms of MIS-C pathogenesis remain poorly understood. 9 Unraveling the pathophysiology of MIS-C requires a better understanding of the underlying immune dysfunctions. Multiple immunological studies have highlighted the contribution of innate immune cells to the systemic inflammation that is characteristic of MIS-C. 4 , 10 For example, severe cardiomyopathy in MIS-C correlates with specific inflammatory gene signatures in monocytes and dendritic cells. 11 In addition, studies on the genetic risk factors for MIS-C overwhelmingly point to innate immune responses as key to its pathogenesis. 12–14 Our current understanding of MIS-C immunology derives from the comprehensive immunological phenotyping of peripheral blood leukocytes in their basal (ie, non-perturbed experimentally) state by transcriptomics and multiparameter flow cytometry. 15–22 Except for a few case reports, 12 , 13 however, studies probing innate immune cell functions in MIS-C are lacking. To characterize innate immune responses in MIS-C, we investigated the responses triggered by engagement of Toll-like receptors (TLR). TLR are membrane proteins that bind molecules produced by pathogens or released by damaged cells and initiate downstream signaling pathways leading to the increased production of antimicrobial mediators, inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, interferons (IFNs), and co-stimulatory molecules, with subsequent development of adaptive immune responses. 23–26 We report that MIS-C is associated with dampened cytokine responses to TLR stimulation and increased expression of negative regulators of TLR signaling. These phenotypes resemble TLR tolerance, a phenomenon characterized by the inability of innate immune cells to respond to further challenge when subjected to excessive or prolonged TLR stimulation. 27 , 28 We also find that among the least TLR-refractory cells are those from children carrying rare variants in the lysosomal trafficking regulator ( LYST ) gene locus. LYST, a multidomain protein implicated in various aspects of vesicular trafficking, affects lysosome morphology and function. 29 , 30 Our work reveals a novel aspect of the innate immune response during MIS-C and points to causative mechanisms and functional requirements. It also identifies genetic determinants of the expression of this refractory state, which may help explain the severity spectrum of the clinical manifestations of MIS-C.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C), Toll-like receptor (TLR) stimulation, LPS (50 ng/ml) stimulation of PBMCs, lysosomal and mitochondrial function, genetic variants (LYST)
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Dysregulated innate immune responses, specifically a lasting TLR hyporesponsiveness or tolerance, contribute to MIS-C. This tolerance may stem from negative feedback induced by high levels of proinflammatory mediators, and/or prolonged stimulation by gut-originated TLR ligands due to increased gut permeability (indicated by elevated zonulin). The mechanism involves increased expression of negative regulators of TLR signaling (e.g., SOCS1, TOLLIP, IRAK-M, SARM1, SHIP-1) which dampen cytokine production. Rare non-synonymous variants in the lysosomal trafficking regulator (LYST) gene are associated with altered lysosomal morphology and function, mitochondrial damage, and shifts in energy metabolism (reduced oxidative phosphorylation, increased glycolysis). These genetic factors influence the immune cells' ability to establish a refractory state to TLR stimulation, with LYST variant carriers exhibiting less TLR hyporesponsiveness and tending towards more severe inflammation.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: TLR tolerance, characterized by innate immune cells' inability to respond to further challenge, is a phenomenon induced by excessive or prolonged TLR stimulation. The study utilized a single dose of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) at 50 ng/mL for PBMC stimulation, with no dose-response comparisons. However, the observed TLR hyporesponsiveness and associated markers persist even months after MIS-C recovery, suggesting a sustained immune alteration rather than a transient, acute dose-dependent effect.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: TLR response downregulation and increased expression of negative regulators of TLR signaling are characteristic of MIS-C and distinguish it from Kawasaki disease, where these changes are not observed. Reduced TLR responsiveness in MIS-C is not due to abnormal TLR4 surface expression. Cells from MIS-C children carrying rare heterozygous variants of lysosomal trafficking regulator (LYST) were specifically found to be less refractory to TLR stimulation and exhibited unique lysosomal/mitochondrial abnormalities and altered energy metabolism. These LYST variant carriers also demonstrated unfavorable clinical inflammatory indicators, highlighting a specific genetic modulation of the immune response in MIS-C and distinguishing them within the MIS-C population.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Children and youth (age ≤21 years) with confirmed Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome in Children (MIS-C), including fully convalescent children months after MIS-C recovery, and a subset carrying rare heterozygous variants of lysosomal trafficking regulator (LYST). Control groups included healthy children, Kawasaki Disease patients, and febrile (non-MIS-C) children. The findings also extend to individuals with pediatric SARS-CoV-2 infection and potential post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC/long COVID).
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Dysregulated innate immune responses, particularly lasting TLR hyporesponsiveness and gut barrier leakage (elevated zonulin), are central to MIS-C pathogenesis. This syndrome is a severe illness involving multi-organ dysfunction following SARS-CoV-2 infection. While TLR hyporesponsiveness might initially limit hyperinflammation, prolonged hyporesponsiveness could increase susceptibility to secondary infections and contribute to long COVID. Rare LYST variants are linked to more severe MIS-C presentations, including profound lymphopenia and higher neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratios, indicating increased risk for severe consequences from SARS-CoV-2 infection.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Adverse risk: for severe illness, multi-organ dysfunction, hyperinflammation, lasting immune dysregulation, gut barrier leakage, and increased severity associated with rare LYST variants and long COVID. Protective benefit: TLR hyporesponsiveness during MIS-C may be protective by limiting hyperinflammation, as reduced hyporesponsiveness in LYST variant carriers correlated with unfavorable inflammatory indicators. Diagnostic/Prognostic utility: TLR hyporesponsiveness, elevated negative regulators of TLR signaling, zonulin levels, CRP, D-dimer, IL-6, and LYST variants can serve as indicators for MIS-C presence, its lasting effects, and disease severity, aiding in identifying children at greatest risk of severe outcomes.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The observational study identifies novel aspects of the innate immune response in MIS-C, pointing to causative mechanisms and functional requirements. TLR response downregulation and increased negative regulators (SOCS1, TOLLIP, SHIP1, SARM1) are reliable characteristics distinguishing MIS-C from Kawasaki disease. The persistence of TLR hyporesponsiveness, increased negative regulators, and elevated zonulin in convalescent MIS-C children suggests these are reliable indicators of lasting immune dysregulation. Assay procedures included normalization steps for reliability in plasma cytokine, zonulin, flow cytometry, oxygen consumption rates (OCR), and extracellular acidification rates (ECAR) measurements. Rare LYST variants are reliably associated with skewed cytokine data distribution, specific cellular abnormalities (lysosomal, mitochondrial, metabolic), and markers of increased disease severity. However, the study was not designed for long-term monitoring, and mechanistic studies are required to test causal associations between hyperinflammation, gut permeability, and TLR tolerance. Further investigations are warranted to validate associations between genotypes and molecular and clinical phenotypes.
